m.c: Walk today with the certainty that the Lord cares for you and will not leave you without what you need. Place in his hands the little you have and you will see his goodness. May his grace go with you and may his peace be your nourishment.
h: The Gospel of Mark tells that Jesus, as he landed, saw a great crowd and had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. He then began to teach them many things. It grew late, and the disciples asked him to send the people away so they could go and buy something to eat in the nearby villages, since the place was deserted.

Jesus answered with a sentence that must have surprised them: “You give them something to eat.” They replied that they had no means to buy bread for so many people. So the Master asked them how many loaves they had, and they went to see. It was five loaves and two fish. It was very little in the face of such a great crowd, but Jesus received them in his hands.

The text says that, taking the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed and broke the loaves and gave them to his disciples to distribute to the crowd. And he divided the two fish among them all. All ate and were satisfied. They picked up twelve baskets full of broken pieces of bread and of the fish. Those who had eaten were five thousand men.

This story teaches us that the little given to Jesus becomes enough. The disciples did not have enough, but they had something, and they placed it in his hands. We also see that God does not give only just what is needed, but provides abundantly: twelve baskets were left over. Even in a deserted place, the Lord can set a table for his people and care for each of his children. That evening, in a remote spot, no one left hungry, and all were witnesses of Jesus' compassion. The disciples learned that day that obeying Jesus, even without understanding everything, opens the door to his provision.
m: It is normal to worry about what is lacking. Sometimes we feel we do not have enough time, enough strength or enough resources for what the day asks of us. The disciples felt the same when they looked at the crowd, then at their five loaves and two fish. And it was precisely there that Jesus taught them a lesson that remains valid today.

Notice that Jesus did not perform the miracle without them. He asked them to bring what they had, then used them to distribute to the crowd. God often acts this way: he takes what we give him, however small it seems, and multiplies it. Your time, your talent, your patience or your little help may be the bread someone needs today.

Apply this with a concrete step. Before going out, ask yourself: what are the five loaves I have today? It may be a free hour, a skill, a word of encouragement or a bit of food to share. Offer it to God in prayer, then look for someone you can bless with it. Do not wait until you have more in order to give; give what you have, with faith, and leave the result in Jesus' hands.

The psalmist invites us: “Taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the one who trusts in him!” To taste is to try, to experience. Today you can test God's faithfulness by believing that he will provide what is needed. There will be moments when you doubt, and it is good to return to him again and again. The same Lord who fed five thousand people in a wilderness will take care of you this day.
o: Lord God, I thank You for the gift of this new day. Thank You for the night's rest, for the roof over my head and for the bread I will have on my table today. Very often I look at what I lack and forget what You have already given me. Today, I want to begin by acknowledging that You are a faithful provider and that Your hand never closes for Your children.

Jesus, You saw the crowd with compassion and did not send them away hungry. Look at me too with that same tenderness. When my resources seem meager, teach me to place them in Your hands, knowing that the little that is given to You can be enough and even left over. Take from me the fear of lack and give me a generous heart, willing to share with those in need.

Help me to taste and see that You are good. Blessed is the one who trusts in You, for those who fear You lack nothing. Guide me in my labors, bless my home and give me wisdom to make good decisions. At the end of this day, may I be able to say that You sustained me by Your grace, and that others saw Your goodness through me. In Jesus' name, amen.

t.c: May the Father who sees in secret give you tonight a quiet sleep and a heart free of resentment. Give him what remained unfinished and rest in his care. His mercy will cover you through the night and welcome you with the light at dawn.
h: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus taught his disciples to pray. Before giving them the prayer, he warned them not to pray like the hypocrites, who loved to do so on street corners to be seen by others. He told them to enter their room, close the door and pray to the Father who is in the secret place, and that the Father, who sees in secret, would reward them.

Then he said to them: “Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” In these first words, Jesus puts God at the center: his name, his kingdom and his will. Before asking anything for ourselves, we learn to look at God as Father.

The prayer continues with simple and profound requests: “Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.” It asks for daily sustenance, forgiveness and protection. These are the needs we all have, in every age and every place.

The most remarkable thing is the language: Jesus said “Our Father,” not “My Father.” He taught us to pray in community, reminding us that we are part of a family. And right after the prayer, he emphasized the importance of forgiving others. This short prayer, which we can recite in a few seconds, contains a whole life of trust, humility and communion with God. Whoever prays it from the heart discovers that God delights to listen to his children, and that his answer is always love. That is why this prayer remains alive after so many centuries on the lips of believers of every language.
m: There are nights when words fail us. We are tired and do not know what to say. For those moments, Jesus left us a prayer we can repeat calmly. The Lord's Prayer is not a magic formula, but a school of prayer where we learn to speak to God as children speak to their father.

You can use this prayer as a guide to close your day. Begin at the beginning: acknowledge God as Father and thank him for what was lived. Then ask for tomorrow's bread, not the whole week's, learning to trust day by day. Next, examine your heart: is there someone you need to forgive? Say it in a low voice and give it to the Lord. Finally, ask for protection for the night and for what is coming.

A simple practice is to pray the Lord's Prayer slowly, pausing a few seconds on each phrase. At “give us this day our daily bread,” give thanks for what you had today. At “forgive us our debts,” honestly name what you want God to forgive you. At “deliver us from evil,” hand over your fears. You will see that so short a prayer can fill the whole heart and bring you deep calm.

The psalmist says that even at night his heart instructs him, and that is why his heart is glad and his body rests secure. You too can end the day with this trust. You do not have to have everything settled, and your prayers do not have to be long. It is enough to come near sincerely. The Father in heaven listens to you, knows you and welcomes you with love every night.
o: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. At the end of this day, I come to You with gratitude, for You have sustained me at every hour. Thank You for today's bread, for health, for my family and for all the little blessings I sometimes let slip by. I acknowledge that You are a Father who is near and who listens to me with love.

Forgive me my trespasses as I also forgive those who have trespassed against me. If someone hurt me today, help me let go of resentment and rest without bitterness. If I failed in my words or attitudes, cleanse me by Your mercy. Deliver me from all evil and lead me not into temptation. May Your kingdom come in my home and Your will be done in my life, on earth as it is in heaven.

I bless the LORD who counsels me; even at night my heart instructs me. I keep the LORD always before me, and that is why I will not be shaken. Therefore my heart is glad and my soul rejoices; my body also will rest secure. Give me deep rest and wake me with renewed hope. Yours are the kingdom, the power and the glory forever. Thank You, Father, for Your constant love. In Jesus' name, amen.
t.s: The Lord's Prayer in the Sermon on the Mount
